slides.title: Article 38 ICJ Statute, quoted in full
slides.text: The lecture opens by re-anchoring treaties in the catalogue of sources: Article 38 lists international conventions first, before custom and general principles. The photograph beside the text is the Peace Palace in The Hague, the seat of the ICJ. Note the same structural point as in the introductory lecture — paragraph (d), judicial decisions and the teachings of publicists, is expressly labelled 'subsidiary means', and applies only 'subject to the provisions of Article 59'.

terms.def: The Statute of the International Court of Justice, annexed to the UN Charter; Article 38 is the conventional catalogue of the sources of international law.

cards.q: Which paragraph of Article 38 ICJ Statute deals with treaties, and how does it describe them?
cards.a: Paragraph (a): international conventions, whether general or particular, establishing rules expressly recognized by the contesting states.

slides.title: The sources, listed
slides.text: The same list as in the introductory lecture, now as the map for this course: treaties, international custom, general principles of law, decisions of international organizations and unilateral acts. Soft law and, separately, teachings and judicial decisions are set apart at the bottom of the slide — visually below the five, because they are not sources in the same sense. Treaties, the first item, are what the remaining seventy slides are about.

cards.q: Which two items on the list of 'sources' are deliberately set apart from the five, and why?
cards.a: Soft law and, separately, teachings and judicial decisions. Soft law is not binding at all; teachings and judicial decisions are subsidiary means for determining the law, not ways of creating it.

slides.title: No hierarchy of norms — except jus cogens
slides.text: Two lines that decide a whole class of exam questions: there is no hierarchy among the sources, and the single exception is jus cogens. The slide gives the standard examples of peremptory norms: the prohibition of torture, apartheid, slavery and genocide. So if a treaty conflicts with custom, neither automatically wins on rank; but if either conflicts with a peremptory norm, the peremptory norm prevails.

terms.def: A peremptory norm from which no derogation is permitted. Slide examples: prohibition of torture, apartheid, slavery, genocide.

cards.q: Is a treaty superior to custom in international law?
cards.a: No — there is no hierarchy among the sources. The only exception is jus cogens, which prevails over all of them.

cards.q: Name the four examples of peremptory norms given in the lecture.
cards.a: The prohibitions of torture, apartheid, slavery and genocide.

slides.title: Conflict of norms: the three rules
slides.text: If rank does not resolve a conflict, these three do. Lex specialis derogat legi generali — the more specific rule displaces the general one. Lex posterior derogat legi priori — the later rule displaces the earlier one. And Article 103 of the UN Charter adds a rule of its own: where obligations under the Charter conflict with obligations under any other international agreement, the Charter prevails. Article 103 is the one to reach for whenever a fact pattern involves the UN.

terms.def: The more specific rule prevails over the more general one.
The later rule prevails over the earlier one.
In a conflict between Charter obligations and obligations under any other international agreement, Charter obligations prevail.

cards.q: A state's obligation under a bilateral treaty conflicts with an obligation under the UN Charter. Which prevails and on what basis?
cards.a: The Charter obligation, under Article 103 of the UN Charter: in the event of a conflict with obligations under any other international agreement, Charter obligations prevail.

cards.q: Which two maxims resolve conflicts between norms of equal rank?
cards.a: Lex specialis derogat legi generali (specific over general) and lex posterior derogat legi priori (later over earlier).

slides.title: Decisions of international organizations: SC Resolution 1973
slides.text: The worked example of a binding IO decision is Security Council Resolution 1973 (2011) on Libya, with a photograph of the vote in the chamber. The extract shows the two formulas that matter: 'Determining that the situation … continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security' and 'Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter'. Those are the conditions and the legal basis on which the Council may bind all states. The recitals also carry the responsibility-to-protect language about protecting the Libyan population.

terms.term: threat to international peace and security
terms.def: The determination under Article 39 UN Charter that opens the Council's Chapter VII powers.

cards.q: Which two elements must appear in a Security Council resolution before it can impose binding obligations?
cards.a: A determination that the situation constitutes a threat to international peace and security, and acting under Chapter VII of the Charter.

slides.title: What a treaty looks like, across three millennia
slides.text: A picture slide with five documents: the Treaty of Osnabrück (Peace of Westphalia) 1648, the Austrian State Treaty 1955, the Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty of 1296 BC carved into a temple wall, and the Treaty of Lisbon 2007 on an EU flag. The point is the range: the form varies from stone relief to a bound volume with wax seals, but the legal category is the same. Note that this slide dates Kadesh to 1296 BC while the introductory lecture said 1280 BC — the discrepancy is in the sources, not in your notes.
slides.note: The Egyptian-Hittite treaty is dated 1296 BC here and 1280 BC in IL01 s006. The course materials are inconsistent about the date; do not rely on it.

slides.title: The twelve questions about a treaty
slides.text: This wheel is the structure of the whole lecture and the best case-solving checklist you will get: 1 legal basis, 2 scope of application of the VCLT, 3 treaty-making power, 4 adoption, 5 entry into force, 6 interpretation, 7 scope of application, 8 treaties and third states, 9 modification, 10 reservations, 11 invalidity, 12 termination and suspension. The wheel reappears throughout the lecture with the current topic highlighted, so it also works as your position marker. Here item 1, legal basis, is highlighted.

cards.q: A problem question turns on a treaty. Which twelve questions does the course checklist ask about it?
cards.a: Legal basis; scope of application of the VCLT; treaty-making power; adoption; entry into force; interpretation; scope of application; treaties and third states; modification; reservations; invalidity; termination and suspension.

slides.title: Definition of a treaty
slides.text: Three elements, and all three must be present: every agreement, between two or more states or subjects of international law, governed by international law. The third element does the work in exam questions — an agreement between two states about buying office furniture under Austrian contract law is not a treaty, because it is not governed by international law. Note also that this general definition says 'or subjects of international law', so it is wider than the VCLT's own definition on the next slides.

terms.def: Every agreement between two or more states or subjects of international law, governed by international law.

cards.q: Two states sign a contract for the purchase of a building, expressly governed by the domestic law of one of them. Is it a treaty?
cards.a: No. The definition requires the agreement to be governed by international law; the parties and the written form are not enough.

cards.q: What are the three elements of the general definition of a treaty?
cards.a: An agreement; between two or more states or subjects of international law; governed by international law.

slides.title: The VCLT: dates that matter
slides.text: The law of treaties is codified in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties of 1969 — and the callout on the slide warns you that 1969 is the date of adoption, not of entry into force. It entered into force only in 1980. Austria acceded in 1979, before entry into force. As of 2023 there are 116 parties, which is well short of the UN's 193 members, and that gap is the reason for the next two slides.

terms.def: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, adopted 1969, in force 1980. Austria acceded in 1979. 116 parties as of 2023.

cards.q: The VCLT is called the 'Vienna Convention of 1969'. What does 1969 refer to, and when did it enter into force?
cards.a: 1969 is the date of adoption. It entered into force only in 1980 — the slide flags this distinction expressly.

slides.title: Who is party to the VCLT
slides.text: The map colours states green for parties, yellow for signatories that have not ratified, and red for non-parties. Green covers most of Europe, much of Africa and South America; conspicuously yellow are the United States and Iran; conspicuously red are France, India, Indonesia, South Africa, Turkey and several others. The lesson is practical: in a case involving a red or yellow state you cannot simply apply the VCLT as a treaty, and you must fall back on customary law — which is exactly what slide 13 says.

cards.q: Why does it matter, in a problem question, whether the states involved are parties to the VCLT?
cards.a: Because the VCLT binds as a treaty only its parties. Many states — including France, India and Turkey — are not parties, so for them the same rules apply only in so far as they are customary international law.

slides.title: Checklist position: scope of application of the VCLT
slides.text: The wheel again, now with item 2 highlighted — the question whether the VCLT applies at all to the agreement in front of you.

slides.title: When the VCLT itself applies
slides.text: The general definition of a treaty on slide 9 is wider than the VCLT's own reach. For the Convention to apply as a convention, the agreement must be concluded between states — not with an international organization — and it must be in written form. Where those conditions fail, the agreement is still a treaty; it is just governed by customary international law instead, and the slide says so in its final line. In practice the two sets of rules largely coincide, because most of the VCLT codifies custom.

cards.q: What are the two additional requirements for the VCLT itself to apply, and what happens when they are not met?
cards.a: The treaty must be concluded between states and must be in written form. If not, the agreement is still a treaty but is governed by customary international law rather than by the Convention.

cards.q: A state and an international organization conclude a written agreement governed by international law. Does the VCLT 1969 apply?
cards.a: Not as a convention — it covers treaties between states. The agreement is still a treaty, governed by customary international law (and by the separate 1986 Vienna Convention where applicable).

slides.title: Bilateral and multilateral treaties
slides.text: The diagram contrasts two circles joined by a single double-headed arrow with five circles joined by arrows to each of the others. The picture makes the practical difference visible: in a bilateral treaty there is one relationship, so a breach or a reservation concerns one partner. In a multilateral treaty each party stands in a relationship with every other, which is why reservations, modification between some parties only, and termination become complicated — the topics numbered 9 to 12 on the wheel.

cards.q: Why do reservations and modification raise problems in multilateral treaties but hardly any in bilateral ones?
cards.a: Because a multilateral treaty creates a separate relationship between every pair of parties. A reservation or a modification alters some of those relationships and not others, whereas a bilateral treaty has only one relationship to alter.

slides.title: Peace of Westphalia 1648, as treaty practice
slides.text: Photographs of the two town halls and the treaty volumes. The slide adds the detail the introductory lecture left out: the peace was made in two places at once because of confession — Osnabrück was the Protestant venue, where the Holy Roman Empire settled with Sweden, and Münster the Catholic one, where Spain settled with the Netherlands and the Empire with France. Two parallel congresses producing linked treaties is an early example of multilateral treaty-making by conference.

slides.title: The Congress of Vienna 1814/15
slides.text: A map of Europe after the Congress, the well-known painting of the delegates, the Acte Final of 1815 with its seals, and a commemorative medal. For the law of treaties the Congress matters as the model of the multilateral peace conference: many states negotiating one instrument together, rather than a web of bilateral settlements. The slide carries no explanatory text of its own.
slides.note: Illustration only; the slide gives no text explaining why the Congress belongs here. The reading above supplies the usual doctrinal context.

slides.title: Self-executing and non-self-executing treaties
slides.text: The second classification of treaties asks whether a provision can be applied by domestic authorities as it stands or whether it first needs implementing legislation. The slide illustrates the non-self-executing type with Article 86 of the Rome Statute: 'States Parties shall … cooperate fully with the Court in its investigation and prosecution of crimes' — an obligation addressed to the state, which must set up its own procedures before anything happens in a domestic courtroom. A self-executing provision, by contrast, is precise enough for a court or an official to apply directly.

terms.def: A treaty provision precise enough to be applied directly by domestic organs, without implementing legislation.
A provision that obliges the state to act but needs domestic implementation before it can be applied to individuals.

cards.q: How do you tell a self-executing treaty provision from a non-self-executing one?
cards.a: By whether the provision is precise enough to be applied directly by domestic organs. If it merely obliges the state to achieve something and needs implementing legislation first — like Article 86 Rome Statute's duty to cooperate — it is non-self-executing.

slides.title: Checklist position: treaty-making power
slides.text: The wheel with item 3 highlighted: who may bind the state.

slides.title: Treaty-making power: the structure
slides.text: The diagram answers one question — who may conclude a treaty for a subject of international law — with three connected propositions. First, subjects of international law themselves stipulate which of their organs may conclude a treaty; international law does not prescribe it. Second, a person may act either on production of full powers or in virtue of their functions, that is by holding an office that carries the authority without a document. Third, if a treaty is concluded without full powers, it is either confirmed by retroactive consent or it is invalid.

terms.def: A document issued by the competent authority designating a person to represent the state for negotiating, adopting or consenting to be bound by a treaty.

cards.q: An official concludes a treaty without full powers and without holding an office that confers them. What are the two possible outcomes?
cards.a: Either the state confirms the act by retroactive consent, or the treaty is invalid.

cards.q: Does international law determine which organ of a state may conclude treaties?
cards.a: No. Subjects of international law stipulate that themselves — international law only asks whether the person could be taken to represent the state.

slides.title: Full powers under Article 7(1) VCLT
slides.text: Article 7(1) gives the two routes in the Convention's own words. Under (a) a person represents the state if they produce appropriate full powers. Under (b) the state may dispense with full powers: authorization can be established from the practice of the state concerned, or from other circumstances showing that the states intended to treat that person as representing the state. So the document is the safe route, and conduct is the fallback.

terms.def: A person represents a state if they produce appropriate full powers, or if it appears from practice or other circumstances that the states so intended.

cards.q: Under Article 7(1) VCLT, how can a person be treated as representing a state without producing full powers?
cards.a: If it appears from the practice of the state concerned, or from other circumstances, that the states intended to consider that person as representing the state for those purposes.

slides.title: Full powers in virtue of a person's functions (Art 7(2) VCLT)
slides.text: Article 7(2) lists who needs no document at all, and the list has a structure worth seeing. Under (a) Heads of State, Heads of Government and Ministers of Foreign Affairs represent the state for everything — the classic 'big three'. Under (b) heads of diplomatic missions and under (c) representatives accredited to a conference or an organization can do far less: they may only adopt the TEXT, and only in that bilateral relationship or in that forum. So an ambassador may adopt a text with the receiving state, but may not thereby bind the state to the treaty.

terms.def: Persons representing their state in virtue of their functions: (a) Head of State, Head of Government, Minister of Foreign Affairs — for all acts; (b) heads of diplomatic missions and (c) accredited representatives — only for adopting the text.

cards.q: Which three office-holders represent their state for all treaty acts without producing full powers?
cards.a: The Head of State, the Head of Government and the Minister of Foreign Affairs (Article 7(2)(a) VCLT).

cards.q: An ambassador signs, on behalf of the sending state, a treaty with the receiving state expressing consent to be bound. Was he competent ex officio?
cards.a: No. Under Article 7(2)(b) a head of mission is considered to represent the state only for adopting the TEXT of a treaty with the receiving state — not for expressing consent to be bound. For that he needs full powers.

slides.title: Cameroon v. Nigeria: Article 46 VCLT, the rule
slides.text: Four slides now quote the ICJ judgment in Cameroon v. Nigeria (Land and Maritime Boundary, 2002), the standard case on what happens when a Head of State binds the state contrary to domestic constitutional rules. The rule is Article 46(1) VCLT: a state may NOT invoke the fact that its consent was expressed in violation of its internal law on competence to conclude treaties — unless that violation was manifest and concerned a rule of internal law of fundamental importance. Article 46(2) defines manifest: objectively evident to any state conducting itself in the matter in accordance with normal practice and in good faith. The Court's conclusion is on the slide: a limitation on a Head of State's capacity is not manifest unless at least properly publicized.

terms.def: Internal law on competence to conclude treaties cannot be invoked to invalidate consent unless the violation was manifest and concerned a rule of fundamental importance.
One that is objectively evident to any state conducting itself in accordance with normal practice and in good faith (Art 46(2) VCLT).

cards.q: State A's president signs a treaty although its constitution requires parliamentary approval. Can State A rely on that to escape the treaty?
cards.a: Only if the violation was manifest and concerned a rule of internal law of fundamental importance (Art 46 VCLT). Per Cameroon v. Nigeria, a limitation on the Head of State's capacity is not manifest unless it has at least been properly publicized.

cards.q: What is the test for a 'manifest' violation under Article 46(2) VCLT?
cards.a: It must be objectively evident to any state conducting itself in the matter in accordance with normal practice and in good faith.

slides.title: Cameroon v. Nigeria: why the Head of State binds fully
slides.text: Nigeria argued that Article 7(2) only establishes that a person has a representative function, not how far that person's powers go. The Court rejected this and relied on the ILC commentary to Article 7(2): Heads of State are considered as representing their state for the purpose of performing ALL acts relating to the conclusion of a treaty. This is what makes the 'big three' different from an ambassador — their authority is not limited to a stage of the procedure.

cards.q: How far does a Head of State's ex officio authority reach under Article 7(2) VCLT, according to Cameroon v. Nigeria?
cards.a: To all acts relating to the conclusion of a treaty — the Court adopted the ILC commentary and rejected the argument that Article 7(2) only establishes the representative function without defining its extent.

slides.title: Cameroon v. Nigeria: no duty to research the other state's constitution
slides.text: Nigeria's second line of argument was that Cameroon knew or ought to have known that its Head of State could not bind Nigeria alone. The Court's answer is the practical heart of the case: there is no general legal obligation for states to keep themselves informed of legislative and constitutional developments in other states. It then read the Nigerian president's 1974 letter and held that the two statements in it could not be regarded as a specific warning that Nigeria would not be bound.

cards.q: Must a state check the constitutional law of its treaty partner before relying on a signature?
cards.a: No. Cameroon v. Nigeria: there is no general legal obligation for states to keep themselves informed of legislative and constitutional developments in other states. That is why Article 46 sets such a high bar.

slides.title: Cameroon v. Nigeria: the holding
slides.text: The Court noted that the two Heads of State had for years resolved boundary difficulties through person-to-person agreements, including Yaoundé II and Maroua, and concluded in paragraph 268 that the Maroua Declaration and the Yaoundé II Declaration must be considered binding and as establishing a legal obligation on Nigeria. Two lessons for an exam answer: a 'declaration' can be a treaty if the parties intended obligations, and prior practice between the parties is evidence of that intention.

terms.def: A 1975 agreement between the Heads of State of Cameroon and Nigeria on the maritime boundary, held binding on Nigeria in ICJ, Cameroon v. Nigeria (2002).

cards.q: A document is titled 'Declaration' and signed by two Heads of State. Can it be a binding treaty?
cards.a: Yes. In Cameroon v. Nigeria the Maroua and Yaoundé II Declarations were held binding and to establish a legal obligation. The title does not decide; the parties' intention, shown here by their established practice, does.

slides.title: Checklist position: adoption of a treaty
slides.text: The wheel with item 4 highlighted: how a treaty text comes into being and how a state becomes bound by it.

slides.title: Simplified procedure: treaty-making without ratification
slides.text: The short route has three stages: negotiations, then optionally initialling, then signature — or an exchange of instruments constituting a treaty. Initialling is marked 'facultative' because it only authenticates the text initialed by the negotiators; it is not consent. In this route signature itself expresses consent to be bound, so the treaty binds from that moment.

terms.def: Optional authentication of a negotiated text by the negotiators' initials; it fixes the text, it does not bind the state.

terms.term: exchange of instruments constituting a treaty
terms.def: A treaty concluded by exchanging notes or letters, without a single signed document.

cards.q: In the simplified procedure, which act makes the state bound?
cards.a: Signature itself (or the exchange of instruments). Initialling only authenticates the text and is optional.

slides.title: A real simplified-procedure treaty
slides.text: The example is an agreement of 20 December 2006 between the Austrian and Hungarian foreign ministers on cooperation at their foreign missions. Its Article 6 shows every feature of the short route at once: it enters into force on the day of signature, it is concluded for an indefinite period, it may be amended by agreement through diplomatic channels, and either party may terminate it in writing through diplomatic channels, with effect three months after receipt. Read the final provisions of any treaty first — they answer questions 5 and 12 on the wheel.

cards.q: Where in a treaty do you look first to answer when it enters into force and how it can be terminated?
cards.a: In its final provisions — as in the Austrian-Hungarian agreement of 2006, whose Article 6 states entry into force on signature, indefinite duration, amendment by agreement, and termination in writing effective three months after receipt.

slides.note: This example slide is in German, unlike the rest of the deck. The exam is written in English.

slides.title: Treaties requiring ratification: five stages
slides.text: The long route adds two stages: negotiations, optional initialling, signature, domestic approval, and finally ratification. The slide marks with a coloured bar that the state is bound only from ratification — signature alone does not bind here. It also marks the stretch between signature and ratification with an arrow labelled 'prohibition to defeat object & purpose': a signatory must not frustrate the treaty in the meantime, even though it is not yet bound by its substance. That interim duty is Article 18 VCLT and it is a favourite exam trap.

terms.def: The international act by which a state establishes its consent to be bound, following domestic approval.

terms.term: obligation not to defeat the object and purpose
terms.def: Between signature and ratification a state must refrain from acts that would defeat the treaty's object and purpose (Art 18 VCLT).

cards.q: State A has signed but not ratified a treaty. Is it free to act as it pleases?
cards.a: No. It is not yet bound by the treaty's substance, but it must refrain from acts that would defeat the object and purpose of the treaty until it makes its intention clear (Art 18 VCLT).

cards.q: Which two stages does the ratification procedure add to the simplified one, and at which point is the state bound?
cards.a: Domestic approval and ratification. The state is bound only upon ratification, not upon signature.

slides.title: Final provisions of the VCLT itself
slides.text: The Convention is its own example. Article 81 opens it for signature to a defined circle of states and sets deadlines; Article 82 makes it subject to ratification, with instruments deposited with the UN Secretary-General; Article 83 keeps it open for accession by the same circle. Accession is the route for a state that did not sign in time — it joins in a single act, with no prior signature. That is how most states, including Austria in 1979, became parties.

terms.def: A single act by which a state becomes party to a treaty it did not sign, deposited with the depositary.
The body that keeps the original text and receives instruments of ratification and accession — for the VCLT, the UN Secretary-General.

cards.q: What is the difference between ratification and accession?
cards.a: Ratification follows a prior signature and completes it. Accession is a single act by which a state that never signed becomes a party, and it is the route left open after the signature period closes.

slides.title: The Austrian procedure, step by step
slides.text: Austria's route through the five stages: negotiations with full powers from the Federal President under Article 50 of the Constitution, signature on the President's full powers, ratification after approval by the National Council and the Federal Council, deposit with the depositary or exchange with the contracting states, entry into application, and finally publication in the Bundesgesetzblatt III. The last two steps are domestic: international entry into force and domestic applicability are separate questions.

terms.def: Bundesgesetzblatt Teil III — the part of the Austrian official gazette in which treaties are published.

slides.title: The Austrian instrument of ratification (1)
slides.text: Two slides reproduce a real Austrian instrument of ratification in German — for the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, BGBl 1972/377. The opening recital records that the convention was opened for signature in New York on 7 March 1966, that its Articles 1, 2 and 14 contain provisions amending the constitution, and that Austria attached a declaration to Article 4.
slides.note: Slides 32–34 are in German; the rest of the deck and the exam are in English.

slides.title: The Austrian instrument of ratification (2)
slides.text: The operative part shows who signs what. After the National Council has given its constitutional approval, the Federal President declares the convention ratified and promises its conscientious fulfilment in the name of the Republic; the instrument is signed by the Federal President, countersigned by the Chancellor and every federal minister, and sealed with the state seal. The point for the law of treaties: ratification is the international act, but it rests on a completed domestic approval procedure.

cards.q: Who signs an Austrian instrument of ratification, and what must have happened first?
cards.a: The Federal President signs, countersigned by the Chancellor and the federal ministers and sealed with the state seal — after the National Council has given its constitutional approval.

slides.title: Erfüllungsvorbehalt: approval with a reservation of implementation
slides.text: A third German slide, and the one with a real doctrinal point. When approving the racial discrimination convention, the National Council resolved under Article 50(2) of the Federal Constitution that it was to be fulfilled by enacting laws. That is the Erfüllungsvorbehalt: parliament approves the treaty but declares that it will not be directly applicable, so courts and authorities cannot apply it until implementing legislation exists. It is the Austrian counterpart of the self-executing / non-self-executing distinction from slide 17. Internationally the treaty entered into force for Austria on 8 June 1972 regardless.

terms.def: Art 50(2) B-VG: parliament's declaration that a treaty is to be implemented by statute, so it is not directly applicable in Austrian law.

cards.q: What does an Erfüllungsvorbehalt change, and what does it not change?
cards.a: It bars direct application of the treaty in domestic law until implementing statutes are passed. It does not affect the treaty's binding force internationally — the state is bound from entry into force either way.

slides.title: The four ways of expressing consent to be bound
slides.text: Signature, where no ratification is required; ratification, defined on the slide as the internal act of approval plus the declaration of acceptance; accession; and exchange of instruments constituting a treaty. Note the composite definition of ratification — it has a domestic half and an international half, which is exactly what the Austrian example on the previous slides showed.

cards.q: List the four means of expressing consent to be bound by a treaty.
cards.a: Signature (where no ratification is required), ratification, accession, and exchange of instruments constituting a treaty.

slides.title: Checklist position: entry into force
slides.text: The wheel with item 5 highlighted.

slides.title: Entry into force — Article 24 VCLT
slides.text: Three rules in descending order. First, the treaty enters into force in the manner and on the date it provides, or as the negotiating states agree — party autonomy comes first. Second, failing any such provision, it enters into force as soon as consent to be bound has been established for ALL the negotiating states. Third, where a state's consent is established after the treaty has already come into force, the treaty enters into force for that state on that later date, unless it provides otherwise. The third paragraph is the seed of the objective/subjective distinction two slides on.

terms.def: Entry into force: as the treaty provides or the negotiating states agree; failing that, when all negotiating states have consented; for later joiners, on the date of their own consent.

cards.q: A treaty says nothing about its entry into force and the negotiating states agreed nothing. When does it enter into force?
cards.a: As soon as consent to be bound has been established for all the negotiating states (Art 24(2) VCLT).

slides.title: The VCLT's own entry-into-force clause (Art 84)
slides.text: Article 84 is the standard pattern for a multilateral treaty: it enters into force on the thirtieth day after the thirty-fifth instrument of ratification or accession is deposited, and for every later state on the thirtieth day after that state's own deposit. Two numbers do the work — a threshold of parties and a waiting period. This is why the VCLT, adopted in 1969, only entered into force in 1980.

slides.title: Objective and subjective entry into force
slides.text: The table compares four treaties — VCLT, UNCLOS, UN-CAT and the Paris Agreement — along the same rows, and its purpose is one distinction. Objective entry into force is the date the treaty comes into force at all, once the required number of ratifications (35, 60, 20, 55 respectively) is reached. Subjective entry into force is the date it comes into force for one particular state. A state that ratified early waits for the threshold: Austria ratified the VCLT on 30.04.1979 but was bound only from 27.01.1980. A state that joins later waits only its own stipulated period: Switzerland deposited in 1990 and was bound thirty days after. Always answer both questions separately in a case.

terms.def: The date on which the treaty enters into force as such, once the required number of ratifications is reached.
The date on which the treaty enters into force for one particular state.

cards.q: State A ratifies a treaty two years before the required number of ratifications is reached. From when is it bound?
cards.a: From the objective entry into force, i.e. when the threshold is met and any waiting period expires — not from its own ratification. Austria ratified the VCLT in April 1979 but was bound from 27 January 1980.

cards.q: What is the difference between objective and subjective entry into force?
cards.a: Objective is the date the treaty enters into force at all; subjective is the date it enters into force for a given state. For a late joiner the two differ.

slides.title: A double threshold: the Paris Agreement
slides.text: Article 21 of the Paris Agreement shows that the threshold need not be a bare headcount. It required at least 55 Parties accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, and then the usual thirty days. The second condition is political engineering: without it a treaty on emissions could have entered into force without the states that actually emit.

cards.q: Why does the Paris Agreement's entry-into-force clause require 55 per cent of emissions and not only 55 parties?
cards.a: Because a bare headcount could be met by states that emit almost nothing, leaving the treaty in force without the major emitters. The double threshold ties entry into force to the states whose conduct the treaty is about.

slides.title: What entry into force triggers: validity
slides.text: The diagram splits the consequences of entry into force into two branches. On the right, timing: the treaty applies from the agreed moment, or if nothing was agreed, from consent by all negotiating parties. On the left, validity, with the two rules to memorise. Article 26 VCLT — pacta sunt servanda: every treaty in force binds the parties and must be performed in good faith. Article 27 — a party may not invoke its internal law as justification for failure to perform. The exception is the one from Cameroon v. Nigeria: a manifest violation of a rule of internal law of fundamental importance regarding competence, Articles 27 and 46 read together.

terms.def: Art 26 VCLT: every treaty in force is binding upon the parties and must be performed by them in good faith.
A party may not invoke the provisions of its internal law as justification for its failure to perform a treaty.

cards.q: A state pleads that its new domestic statute makes performance of a treaty impossible. Is that a defence?
cards.a: No. Article 27 VCLT: internal law may not be invoked as justification for failure to perform. The only opening is Article 46 — a manifest violation of a rule of internal law of fundamental importance concerning competence to conclude treaties, which goes to validity of consent, not to performance.

cards.q: State the rule of Article 26 VCLT in its Latin name and in substance.
cards.a: Pacta sunt servanda: every treaty in force is binding upon the parties to it and must be performed by them in good faith.

slides.title: Checklist position: interpretation
slides.text: The wheel with item 6 highlighted — how the text of a treaty is to be read.

slides.title: Who interprets a treaty
slides.text: Before the method comes the question of the interpreter, and the default answer is uncomfortable: interpretation is decentralized, meaning each party interprets for itself. Some treaties fix that by creating an organ competent to interpret, or by sending disputes to a court or arbitral tribunal. Two examples on the slide: Article 32 ECHR gives the European Court of Human Rights jurisdiction over all matters concerning interpretation and application of the Convention, and Article 1 of the Optional Protocol to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations puts such disputes under the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ.

terms.def: Each party interprets the treaty for itself; there is no general authoritative interpreter in international law.

cards.q: Who is competent to interpret a treaty if the treaty says nothing about it?
cards.a: Each party for itself — interpretation is decentralized. An authoritative interpreter exists only where the treaty creates one, such as the ECtHR under Article 32 ECHR or the ICJ under the Optional Protocol to the VCCR.

slides.title: Article 31 VCLT: the general rule
slides.text: Two framing statements first: all methods are of equal rank — there is no hierarchy of canons, and the approach is objective, oriented towards the text — and everything happens in good faith. Then the four elements: (a) the ordinary meaning of the terms; (b) the context, which the Convention defines to include the preamble and annexes, any agreement made between all the parties in connection with the conclusion, and any instrument made by one or more parties and accepted by the others as related to the treaty; (c) subsequent agreements, subsequent practice, and any relevant rules of international law applicable between the parties; and (d) the object and purpose, which carries effet utile and implied powers with it.

terms.def: A treaty should be read so that its provisions have practical effect rather than none.
Powers not written into the constituent instrument but necessary for an organization to perform its functions; a teleological reading.

cards.q: Is the ordinary meaning of the words the primary method of treaty interpretation under Article 31 VCLT?
cards.a: It is the starting point, but all the methods are of equal rank — ordinary meaning, context, subsequent agreement and practice, and object and purpose are applied together in good faith as a single operation.

cards.q: What counts as 'context' under Article 31(2) VCLT?
cards.a: The treaty text with its preamble and annexes, any agreement made between all the parties in connection with the conclusion of the treaty, and any instrument made by one or more parties and accepted by the others as related to it.

slides.title: Interpretation as a diagram
slides.text: The same rule drawn as three branches from the node '6. Interpretation'. Ordinary meaning stands alone on top. Systematic interpretation splits into Article 31(2) — treaty text with preamble and attachments, plus every agreement or document by the parties made on the occasion of the conclusion — and Article 31(3) — subsequent agreements, uniform subsequent practice by all the parties, and any relevant rules of international law between them, with Article 103 of the UN Charter given as the example. Teleological interpretation carries effet utile and implied powers, and the diagram flags that implied powers matter especially for international organizations.

cards.q: Under Article 31(3) VCLT, whose subsequent practice counts?
cards.a: Uniform practice by all the parties to the treaty — the practice of one or a few parties is not enough to establish an agreed interpretation.

slides.title: A worked example: the VCCR preamble
slides.text: The next two slides take one provision and show interpretation in action. This one is the preamble of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations 1963 — the parties recall the purposes of the UN Charter on sovereign equality and friendly relations and state their belief that a convention on consular relations would contribute to friendly relations among nations irrespective of differing constitutional and social systems. Under Article 31(2) the preamble is part of the context, so these sentences are legitimate material for reading Article 36.

slides.title: Article 36(1)(b) VCCR: the provision being interpreted
slides.text: The text itself: if a detained foreign national so requests, the authorities of the receiving state must without delay inform the consular post of the sending state, must forward any communication from the detainee to the consulate, and — the words the slide emphasises — must inform the person concerned without delay of HIS RIGHTS under the subparagraph. That last phrase is why the provision is famous: read with the preamble and the object and purpose, it was held to give rights to the individual and not only to the sending state, which is what the LaGrand and Avena litigation before the ICJ turned on.

terms.def: Art 36(1)(b) VCCR: on request, the receiving state must inform the detainee's consulate without delay and must inform the detainee of that right.

cards.q: Why is the phrase 'shall inform the person concerned without delay of his rights' in Art 36(1)(b) VCCR significant?
cards.a: Because it is textual evidence that the provision confers rights on the individual, not only on the sending state — the reading that the preamble and the object and purpose of the Convention support.

slides.title: Checklist position: scope of application
slides.text: The wheel with item 7 highlighted, and it branches into two questions that must be asked separately: the temporal scope of application — from when and until when does the treaty apply — and the territorial scope — to which territories.

slides.title: Territorial scope, published in the gazette
slides.text: A German-language announcement from the Austrian Bundesgesetzblatt of 18 August 2011: the Chancellor announces the Geltungsbereich — the scope of application — of the UN Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, recording that Benin deposited its instrument of accession on 29 July 2011. The practical lesson: for a multilateral treaty the circle of parties changes over time, and the answer to 'does this treaty apply between these two states' is looked up in such lists, not assumed.

slides.title: Temporal scope: a termination clause read closely
slides.text: Article 15 of the bilateral investment treaty between Austria and Kuwait shows how carefully treaties handle their own end. Paragraph 1: the agreement runs for thirty years and renews automatically for like periods unless a party gives written notice one year before the expiry of a period. Paragraph 2 is the survival clause: for investments made before the termination takes effect, the agreement's provisions continue to apply for a further twenty years. So a treaty can go on producing legal effects two decades after it has been terminated — a favourite trap in a fact pattern with dates.

terms.def: A provision keeping a treaty's protections in force for existing situations for a stated period after termination.

cards.q: A BIT is terminated in 2020. An investment was made in 2015. Until when can the investor rely on the treaty, under a clause like Article 15 Austria-Kuwait?
cards.a: For twenty years from termination, i.e. until 2040 — the survival clause keeps the provisions effective for investments made before the notice took effect.

slides.title: Checklist position: treaties and third states
slides.text: The wheel with item 8 highlighted.

slides.title: Pacta tertiis nec nocent nec prosunt
slides.text: The rule and its two qualifications. Agreements neither harm nor benefit third parties; a treaty produces effects for a third state only if that state consents. The asymmetry is what to remember: where the treaty benefits the third state, consent is assumed; where it imposes an obligation, consent must be in writing. The reason is obvious once stated — nobody objects to being given a right, but nobody may be burdened without a clear act of will.

terms.term: pacta tertiis nec nocent nec prosunt
terms.def: Treaties neither harm nor benefit third parties; effects for a third state require its consent.

cards.q: Treaty A-B grants a right to state C and imposes a duty on state D. What consent does each require?
cards.a: For C the consent is presumed, because the treaty confers a benefit. For D consent must be given in writing, because the treaty imposes an obligation.

slides.title: Checklist position: modification of treaties
slides.text: The wheel with item 9 highlighted, branching into three words the lecture distinguishes: revision, amendment and modification.

slides.title: Checklist position: reservations
slides.text: The wheel with item 10 highlighted. The small chart beside it shows the percentage of state parties with at least one reservation for a series of human rights treaties — the values run from roughly a tenth to over half, which is the point: reservations are not an exception but ordinary practice in multilateral treaty-making.
slides.note: The chart's axis labels are too small to read reliably at slide resolution; the individual treaty values are not reproduced here.

slides.title: What a reservation is (Art 2(1)(d) VCLT)
slides.text: A reservation is a unilateral statement by which a state purports to change how the treaty applies to it, and it comes in only two shapes: excluding a certain provision altogether, or modifying the legal effect of a certain provision. What matters is the substance, not the label — a statement called an 'interpretative declaration' is a reservation if it excludes or modifies legal effect.

terms.def: Art 2(1)(d) VCLT: a unilateral statement made on signing, ratifying or acceding, purporting to exclude or modify the legal effect of certain treaty provisions for that state.

cards.q: What are the only two things a reservation can do?
cards.a: Exclude a certain provision of the treaty, or modify the legal effect of a certain provision — for the reserving state.

slides.title: When a reservation is prohibited (Art 19 VCLT)
slides.text: Three cases, and they run from explicit to implicit. Under (a) the treaty itself prohibits reservations. Under (b) the treaty permits only specified reservations and the one made is not among them. Under (c) — the residual and by far the most litigated — the reservation is incompatible with the object and purpose of the treaty. The first question in any reservation problem is Article 19; only if the reservation clears it do you move on to its effects.

terms.def: A reservation is prohibited if the treaty forbids reservations, if it allows only specified ones and this is not among them, or if it is incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose.

cards.q: A treaty is silent about reservations and a state makes one that guts its central obligation. Is it permissible?
cards.a: No — Article 19(c) VCLT: a reservation incompatible with the object and purpose of the treaty is prohibited even where the treaty says nothing about reservations.

cards.q: Name the three grounds on which Article 19 VCLT prohibits a reservation.
cards.a: (a) the treaty prohibits reservations; (b) the treaty allows only specified reservations and this is not one of them; (c) the reservation is incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose.

slides.title: How reservations become public
slides.text: A German-language page of the Austrian gazette listing the reservations and declarations made by other states to the racial discrimination convention. Egypt declared that it does not consider itself bound by Article 22, under which disputes about interpretation go to the ICJ at the request of one party, and insisted that the consent of all parties to the dispute is needed in each case. Denmark declared that the local government of the Faroe Islands must first approve the implementing legislation. The practical point: reservations by OTHER states are part of the legal position you must check, and they are published exactly like the treaty.

slides.title: Saudi Arabia's reservation to CEDAW
slides.text: The worked example, in two parts. First a general reservation: in case of contradiction between any term of the Convention and the norms of Islamic law, the Kingdom is not under an obligation to observe the contradictory terms. Second, specific reservations to Article 9(2) — equal rights of women with respect to the nationality of their children — and Article 29(1), the dispute settlement clause. Read this against Article 19(c) and ask yourself what is left of the Convention if a party may set aside any term that conflicts with an unspecified body of other norms.

terms.def: Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979).
A reservation referring to a whole body of domestic or religious law rather than to identified provisions; criticised as too imprecise to assess.

cards.q: Why is a reservation subordinating a human rights treaty to 'the norms of Islamic law' problematic under Article 19 VCLT?
cards.a: Because it does not specify which provisions it affects, so its extent cannot be assessed — and to the extent it releases the state from obligations essential to the treaty's object and purpose it is incompatible with them under Article 19(c).

slides.title: The legal effect of a reservation: four reactions
slides.text: This diagram is the heart of the reservations topic; learn it as a decision tree. A reservation can be met with explicit acceptance (Art 20(4)(a)) or tacit acceptance (Art 20(5), silence for twelve months) — both create treaty relations between the accepting and the reserving state, with the provisions modified to the extent of the reservation under Article 21. Or it can be met with an objection, and everything turns on the objection's form. An UNQUALIFIED objection does not intend to preclude entry into force: the treaty applies between the two states, but under Article 21(3) the provision to which the reservation relates does not apply between them to the extent of the reservation. A QUALIFIED objection does preclude entry into force: under Article 20(4)(b) there are no treaty relations between those two states at all.

terms.def: Art 20(5): a reservation is considered accepted if no objection is raised within twelve months of notification, or by the date of consent to be bound, whichever is later.
An objection that does not preclude entry into force; the treaty applies between the two states minus the reserved provision (Art 21(3)).
An objection stating that it precludes entry into force; no treaty relations arise between objector and reserving state (Art 20(4)(b)).

cards.q: State A reserves Article 5. State B objects but says the objection does not preclude entry into force. What applies between A and B?
cards.a: The treaty applies between them, except that Article 5 does not apply as between A and B to the extent of the reservation (Art 21(3) VCLT).

cards.q: State C says nothing about state A's reservation for over a year. What is the effect?
cards.a: Tacit acceptance under Article 20(5) VCLT. Treaty relations arise between A and C with the reserved provision modified to the extent of the reservation (Art 21).

cards.q: What is the difference between a qualified and an unqualified objection to a reservation?
cards.a: A qualified objection precludes the entry into force of the treaty between the objecting and the reserving state (Art 20(4)(b)). An unqualified one leaves the treaty in force between them, minus the reserved provision (Art 21(3)).

slides.title: Austria's objection to the Saudi reservation
slides.text: The Austrian objection of 21 August 2001 is the same decision tree applied to real facts. Austria reasons that the reservation to Islamic law does not clearly specify which provisions it covers or the extent of the derogation, which raises doubts about the commitment; that a final assessment of admissibility cannot be made without clarification; and that the reservation is inadmissible in so far as it negatively affects compliance with obligations essential to the object and purpose. It objects separately to the reservation to Article 9(2) as incompatible with object and purpose. And it closes with the decisive sentence: this position does not preclude the entry into force in its entirety of the Convention between Saudi Arabia and Austria — an unqualified objection.

cards.q: Austria objected to Saudi Arabia's CEDAW reservation but added that its position 'does not preclude the entry into force in its entirety of the Convention' between them. What type of objection is that, and what follows?
cards.a: An unqualified objection. The Convention is in force between the two states; the provisions covered by the reservation do not apply between them to the extent of the reservation (Art 21(3) VCLT).

slides.title: Checklist position: invalidity of treaties
slides.text: The wheel with item 11 highlighted, branching into two questions to keep apart: the grounds of invalidity, and the procedure for invoking it.

slides.title: Invalidity for lack of consent
slides.text: The first family of grounds concerns defects in who consented. One is the manifest violation of a rule of domestic law of fundamental importance — Article 46, met already in Cameroon v. Nigeria. The other is acts of a person lacking competence to represent the state, which splits in two: violation of internal law governing competence, and failure to observe a restriction on the representative's authority. The slide flags the condition for the second with an exclamation mark: notification is needed — the restriction can only be invoked if it was notified to the other negotiating states beforehand.

terms.def: A specific limitation on a representative's power; it can be invoked as invalidating consent only if notified to the other negotiating states before consent was expressed (Art 47 VCLT).

cards.q: A state instructs its negotiator not to accept a particular clause; the negotiator accepts it anyway. Can the state rely on the restriction?
cards.a: Only if the restriction was notified to the other negotiating states before the negotiator expressed consent. Without prior notification it cannot be invoked as invalidating consent.

slides.title: The other grounds of invalidity
slides.text: Five more, in ascending order of gravity: error, meaning a mistaken impression of facts that vitiates consent; fraud and corruption; coercion of a representative of a state; coercion of a state by the threat or use of force; and incompatibility with jus cogens. The photograph is of Emil Hácha with Hitler and Göring in Berlin in 1939 — the textbook case of coercion of a representative, the night the Czechoslovak president was pressed into signing away what remained of his state. Note the difference between the third and fourth ground: coercion of the person, versus coercion of the state itself.

terms.def: A mistaken impression of facts which vitiates consent to a treaty.
Pressure directed at the person negotiating or signing; the classic example is Hácha in Berlin, 1939.
Procuring a treaty by the threat or use of force against the state itself.

cards.q: Distinguish coercion of a representative from coercion of a state as grounds of invalidity.
cards.a: Coercion of a representative targets the individual negotiating or signing (Hácha, Berlin 1939). Coercion of a state is the threat or use of force against the state itself to procure the treaty. Both invalidate, but they are separate grounds.

cards.q: List the grounds of invalidity of a treaty other than lack of competence.
cards.a: Error, fraud and corruption, coercion of a representative, coercion of a state by threat or use of force, and incompatibility with jus cogens.

slides.title: Checklist position: termination and suspension
slides.text: The wheel with item 12 highlighted — the last question on the list.

slides.title: Termination and suspension
slides.text: Obligations can stop in two ways, and the diagram reduces the difference to one word each: termination is final, suspension is temporary. Everything that follows — the grounds, the procedure — attaches to one or the other, so in a case always say which of the two is being claimed.

cards.q: What separates termination from suspension of a treaty?
cards.a: Termination ends the obligations finally; suspension stops them temporarily, after which they revive.

slides.title: Termination in bilateral and multilateral treaties
slides.text: The same event has different names depending on the treaty. In a bilateral treaty one party's exit ends the treaty — termination. In a multilateral treaty one party's exit is withdrawal, and the treaty continues among the rest. This follows from the picture on slide 14: a bilateral treaty is one relationship, a multilateral treaty is many.

terms.def: One party's exit from a multilateral treaty; the treaty remains in force among the other parties.

cards.q: A party leaves a multilateral treaty. Is the treaty terminated?
cards.a: No — that is withdrawal. The treaty remains in force between the remaining parties. Termination is what the equivalent act does to a bilateral treaty.

slides.title: Three routes to discontinuance
slides.text: Obligations may end in conformity with the provisions of the treaty itself — the termination clause, as in the Austrian-Kuwaiti investment treaty; by consent of the parties, which is available at any time regardless of what the treaty says; or on grounds drawn from customary international law, which are listed two slides on. Check them in that order: the text first, then agreement, then the customary grounds as a last resort.

cards.q: In which order do you check the routes by which treaty obligations may end?
cards.a: First the treaty's own provisions; then consent of the parties, available at any time; then the grounds of customary international law.

slides.title: The termination clause again
slides.text: Article 15 of the Austria-Kuwait investment treaty is shown a second time, now as the illustration of the first route — termination in conformity with the provisions of the treaty. Thirty years, automatic renewal, one year's written notice before the end of a period, and the twenty-year survival clause for existing investments.

slides.title: The customary grounds of termination
slides.text: Four grounds that operate even where the treaty is silent. Material breach — a serious violation by one party entitles the other to terminate or suspend. Supervening impossibility of performance — the object of the treaty has permanently disappeared. Clausula rebus sic stantibus, a fundamental change of circumstances, which is deliberately hard to invoke: the changed circumstances must have been an essential basis of consent and the change must radically transform the extent of the obligations. And desuetude or obsolescence, where the parties' conduct shows the treaty has fallen out of use.

terms.def: A serious violation entitling the other party to invoke it as a ground for terminating or suspending the treaty.
Fundamental change of circumstances; admissible only where the circumstances were an essential basis of consent and the change radically transforms the obligations.
A treaty falling out of use by the conduct of the parties.

cards.q: A state argues that economic conditions have changed dramatically and it can no longer afford a treaty. Will clausula rebus sic stantibus help?
cards.a: Almost certainly not. The changed circumstances must have been an essential basis of the parties' consent and the change must radically transform the extent of obligations still to be performed; hardship or a bad bargain is not enough.

cards.q: Name the four customary grounds for discontinuing treaty obligations.
cards.a: Material breach, supervening impossibility of performance, fundamental change of circumstances (clausula rebus sic stantibus), and desuetude or obsolescence.

slides.title: The checklist, closed
slides.text: The wheel one last time with nothing highlighted — all twelve questions have now been worked through. Use it as the skeleton for any treaty problem: legal basis, scope of the VCLT, treaty-making power, adoption, entry into force, interpretation, scope of application, third states, modification, reservations, invalidity, termination.
